title: Office Holiday Party Drinking: How to Pace Yourself at an Open Bar
excerpt: How to enjoy the work Christmas party without overdoing it: how much is sensible, open bar pacing, saying no gracefully, getting home safely, and the morning after.
metaDescription: How to handle drinking at the office Christmas party: a sensible limit, open bar pacing, turning down drinks, getting home safely, and the next morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** the best way to handle drinking at an office holiday party is to decide your limit before you walk in, eat a real meal first, and alternate every alcoholic drink with water or a soft drink. For most people that means two or three drinks spread across the evening, which is enough to enjoy yourself and still be someone your coworkers are glad they talked to on Monday. An open bar removes the price signal that normally slows you down, so you need a plan to replace it.

**The quick rules:** Eat before you go. Have your first drink be a non-alcoholic one. Hold one drink at a time and let it last. Switch to water or a mocktail after your second drink, then reassess. Skip shots and anything you can't easily measure, like punch. Know how you're getting home before you have your first sip. And if a colleague is passed out, confused, or vomiting and can't stay awake, treat it as a medical problem, not an embarrassment.

> **When a night out becomes a medical problem.** Most holiday parties end with nothing worse than a tired morning. But **call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away** if someone can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, has blue or very pale skin, feels cold to the touch, or is vomiting while barely conscious. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, which can be fatal. Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off," and don't try to sober them up with coffee or a cold shower. If they're lying down, roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit. **For your own health, see a doctor** if you have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, vomit that contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, or you can't keep fluids down the next day.

## Why the Office Holiday Party Is Harder to Navigate Than a Normal Night Out

A work holiday party looks like any other party, but it stacks the deck in a few specific ways.

**The drinks are free.** At a bar, every round costs money, and that small decision point slows most people down. An open bar removes it. You can go from one drink to four without ever reaching for your wallet, and bartenders at catered events often pour generously because they're trying to keep a line moving.

**The schedule encourages drinking on an empty stomach.** Many office parties start straight after work, sometimes with drinks served before the food comes out. If you skipped a proper lunch because of end-of-year deadlines, you can be several drinks in before you've eaten anything more than a few passed appetizers.

**Nerves push the pace.** Talking to the CEO, your manager's manager, or people from departments you never deal with can be stressful. A drink in hand gives you something to do, and it's easy to sip faster when you're anxious.

**People top you up.** Servers refill glasses of wine before they're empty, and colleagues buy (or fetch) rounds. When your glass never empties, you lose track of how much you've actually had.

**The stakes are different.** At a friend's party, an overly loud story is forgotten by morning. At work, people remember, and some of them have influence over your projects, reviews, and promotions. That isn't a reason to be anxious all night. It's a reason to stay in the zone where you're relaxed but still in control.

None of this means you shouldn't drink. Plenty of people have a couple of glasses of wine, have a good time, and never think about it again. The goal of this guide is to help you do exactly that.

## Christmas Party Drinking: How Much Is Sensible?

There's no single right number, because alcohol affects people differently depending on body size, sex, what you've eaten, how tired you are, any medications you take, and how often you normally drink. But some general reference points help.

In the US, a **standard drink** contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. That's roughly:

- 12 ounces of regular beer (about 5% alcohol)
- 5 ounces of wine (about 12% alcohol)
- 1.5 ounces of spirits like vodka, gin, or whiskey (about 40% alcohol)

The catch at parties is that very few drinks are exactly one standard drink. A large wine glass filled generously can hold two. A craft IPA can be 7% to 9% alcohol. A cocktail with two kinds of spirits can be two or three standard drinks in one glass. Holiday punch and eggnog are notoriously hard to judge, because you can't see how much rum went into the bowl.

The US Dietary Guidelines describe moderate drinking as up to two drinks in a day for men and up to one for women, and they note that drinking less is better for health than drinking more. Binge drinking is usually defined by the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) as a pattern that brings blood alcohol up to 0.08%, which typically happens after about five drinks for men or four for women within roughly two hours.

A practical way to use this at a work party: **pick a number before you arrive, and make it a number you'd be comfortable with your boss seeing.** For many people that's two or three drinks across a three- or four-hour event. Your liver clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though that varies from person to person, so spacing matters as much as the total.

## Before the Party: Set Yourself Up

Most of the work happens before you get there.

### Eat a real meal

Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol passes into the small intestine, where most of it is absorbed. That means a slower, lower peak in blood alcohol compared with drinking on an empty stomach. This is one of the most reliable findings in alcohol research, and it's the single easiest thing you can do.

You don't need anything special. A normal meal with protein, some fat, and fiber works well: a chicken and grain bowl, eggs and toast, a sandwich and soup. Eat it an hour or two before the party, not instead of the party food, but in addition to it. Our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide) goes through the best options in detail.

### Hydrate during the day

Alcohol makes you urinate more by suppressing a hormone (vasopressin) that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Starting the evening already dehydrated after a day of coffee and back-to-back meetings makes the next morning worse. Drink water through the afternoon so you arrive in a normal state.

### Plan your route home

Decide how you're getting home before you have your first drink. Book a rideshare, check the last train, arrange to share a cab, or confirm the designated driver. Once you've had a few drinks, your judgment about whether you're "fine to drive" becomes unreliable, which is exactly why the decision should be made earlier. Many companies offer rides or reimburse taxis for holiday parties; check the invitation or ask HR.

### Know your medications

Some common medicines don't mix well with alcohol. Antihistamines, sleep aids, some antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines, opioid pain relievers, and certain antibiotics can increase drowsiness or cause other reactions. If you take any regular prescription, check the label or ask a pharmacist before the party. This matters even more if you're on something new.

### Give yourself a reason to leave on time

If you have an early start the next day, a dinner reservation, or a babysitter waiting, you have a natural exit point. People are rarely offended when someone leaves at a reasonable hour; they're far more likely to remember someone who stayed too long.

## Open Bar Pacing: How Not to Get Drunk at the Office Party

This is the heart of it. An open bar isn't a problem if you treat it like a pharmacy rather than a buffet.

### Start with a non-alcoholic drink

Your first drink sets the tone. Ask for sparkling water with lime, a soda, or a mocktail when you arrive. You're thirsty after the commute, you're a bit nervous, and the first drink is usually the one people finish fastest. Make that one alcohol-free and you've bought yourself time to settle in.

### Alternate every drink

After each alcoholic drink, have a full glass of water or a soft drink before the next one. This roughly halves how much you drink over the evening without anyone noticing, keeps something in your hand, and helps with the dehydration side of a hangover. It won't cancel out the alcohol, but it slows your pace, and pace is most of what matters. (For more on what water does and doesn't do, see [does water help a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover).)

### One drink at a time, and let it last

Never double-fist, and don't accept a new drink while you still have one. If someone offers to get you another, it's completely fine to say "I'm good, thanks, still working on this one." Aim to make each drink last at least an hour. Sipping, not gulping.

### Choose drinks you can measure

Simple drinks make counting easy:

- A bottle or can of beer (check the strength; light lagers are easier to pace than strong craft beers)
- A glass of wine, ideally a smaller pour
- A highball, like a gin and tonic or whiskey and soda, with one measured shot of spirit

Harder to track:

- Punch and eggnog, where you can't see the alcohol content
- Large cocktails or anything with multiple spirits
- Shots, which deliver a full standard drink in seconds
- Wine that gets topped up by servers before you finish

If wine keeps getting refilled, finish the glass and then put your hand over it or turn it down when the server comes by. Or simply leave a little in the glass so it looks full enough.

### Be careful with bubbles

Sparkling wine and champagne are fixtures at holiday events. Some small studies suggest carbonation can speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed, though the effect varies between people. Either way, a flute of prosecco is easy to drink quickly. Treat it like any other drink: one counts as one, and it should last a while. Our guide to [champagne hangovers](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) covers why some people find bubbly hits them harder.

### Skip the shots

Shots are where office parties go wrong. Someone suggests a round, the group cheers, and suddenly everyone has had a quick extra drink or two on top of whatever they were sipping. You can join the moment without drinking: hold a shot glass of water, toast with your current drink, or simply say "I'll cheer with this one." Nobody keeps score.

### Eat throughout the night

Don't let the appetizers pass you by. Eating steadily through the evening keeps slowing down absorption. Prioritize the substantial options: meatballs, sliders, cheese, skewers, bread. A plate of food also gives your hands something to do besides holding a drink.

### Check in with yourself halfway

Around the midpoint of the event, take a moment, maybe on a trip to the restroom, and ask yourself honestly: How many drinks have I had? Am I talking louder or faster than usual? Do I feel the warm, loosened-up glow, or am I past it? If you're at or near your number, switch to non-alcoholic drinks for the rest of the night. This is the single most useful habit for any party.

## Saying No (or "Not Right Now") Without Making It a Thing

Most people worry far more about turning down a drink than anyone else does. At work, many colleagues are pacing themselves too, driving, pregnant, on medication, in recovery, or simply not interested in drinking. A non-alcoholic drink in hand is the easiest way to avoid questions, because people rarely ask what's in your glass.

If someone does push, short and friendly works best:

- "I'm driving tonight."
- "I've got an early start tomorrow."
- "I'm pacing myself, but cheers!"
- "I'm good for now, thanks."

You don't owe anyone an explanation. If a manager or senior colleague keeps pressing drinks on people, that's worth noting; good managers don't do this, and HR teams generally don't want it happening either.

## Work Party Etiquette: The Professional Side of Drinking

The reason office party drinking deserves its own guide is that the consequences extend past the next morning. A few principles keep you on the right side of things.

### Remember it's still a work event

Even at an offsite venue after hours, a company-hosted party is generally treated as a work event. Your company's conduct policies, including those on harassment and respectful behavior, still apply. Alcohol doesn't change that, and "I'd had a few" is not a defense anyone accepts.

### Avoid the classic mistakes

The things people most often regret after an office party are predictable:

- Complaining about the company, a manager, or a colleague
- Discussing salaries, layoffs, or confidential projects
- Flirting with or touching coworkers, especially anyone junior or anyone you have influence over
- Getting into an argument about politics
- Posting photos or videos of colleagues without asking
- Being the last person standing at the bar

If you notice yourself wanting to do any of these, that's a good signal you've reached your limit.

### Use the party for what it's good at

The upside of a holiday party is real. It's one of the few times you can talk casually with people from other teams or with senior leaders. The best version of you at that party is relaxed, curious, and asks good questions. That version is usually one or two drinks in, not five. For a broader look at how alcohol affects your work life, see our guide to [alcohol and work performance](/never-hungover/alcohol-work-performance-professional-impact-guide-2025).

### Look out for others

If a colleague seems to be drinking far more than usual or getting unsteady, a quiet "Hey, want to grab some food with me?" or "Let's get some water" is kind and often enough. Help them find a ride home rather than letting them drive. If someone seems seriously unwell, use the emergency signs at the top of this page and get help.

## The After-Party Question

Many office parties end with someone suggesting "one more" at a nearby bar. This is where good evenings go sideways. You're already a few drinks in, the professional structure of the event is gone, the drinks now cost money (which ironically sometimes speeds things up, because rounds get bought), and it's later than you planned.

Before you agree, ask yourself whether you'd be happy to tell your manager about it on Monday. If the answer is yes, go, but switch to non-alcoholic drinks or set a strict one-drink limit. If you have work the next morning, the cleanest move is to head home. Nobody remembers who left at 10 p.m.; everybody remembers who was still there at 2 a.m.

## Getting Home Safely

This deserves its own section because it's the most serious risk of the night. Never drive after drinking, even if you "feel fine." Alcohol affects reaction time and judgment before you notice obvious signs of being drunk, and a DUI or crash is a life-changing outcome. Use the plan you made before the party. If your plan falls through, ask a sober colleague, call a rideshare or taxi, or ask the event organizer; many companies are prepared for exactly this.

If you're walking or taking public transit, travel with someone if you can, keep your phone charged, and let a friend or partner know when you've left.

## The Morning After: Going to Work With a Hangover

Many office holiday parties happen on a weeknight, which means some people walk into the office the next day feeling rough. If that's you:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Water first. If you were sick or sweating, an electrolyte drink can help replace salts.
- **Eat breakfast.** Even if you're not hungry, toast, eggs, a banana, or oatmeal helps settle your stomach and raise your blood sugar.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Ibuprofen or aspirin can irritate a stomach that's already inflamed from alcohol, so take them with food. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver, so stick to a single standard dose, never more than the label allows. Our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Show up on time.** Arriving late and visibly hungover is far more noticeable than whatever happened at the party.
- **Don't drive if you might still be over the limit.** If you drank heavily late into the night, there may still be alcohol in your system in the morning. Your body clears it at a fairly fixed rate, and coffee, cold showers, and sleep don't speed that up.
- **Skip the "hair of the dog."** Another drink only postpones the hangover. We look at the evidence in [does hair of the dog work](/never-hungover/does-hair-of-the-dog-work).

For the full rundown, our [hangover prevention guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence behind them.

## If You Did Overdo It

It happens. If you wake up worried about something you said or did, a few steps help:

1. **Don't panic or overthink.** Most people were paying far less attention to you than you think.
2. **If you know you upset or offended someone, apologize briefly and sincerely.** "I'm sorry about last night; I was out of line" is usually enough. Don't make a long production of it.
3. **If something serious happened,** such as a conflict with a manager or behavior that could be a policy issue, it's often better to raise it yourself, calmly, than to wait for it to come up.
4. **Take a look at your plan for next time.** What pushed you past your limit: an empty stomach, shots, the after-party? Fix that one thing.

If you find you regularly drink more than you intend to, at work events or elsewhere, that's worth talking over with your doctor. It's a common experience and a normal thing to bring up at a check-up.

## Myths About Holiday Party Drinking

**"Beer before liquor, never sicker."** A 2019 study published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* had volunteers drink beer then wine, wine then beer, or just one of the two, and found that the order made no meaningful difference to how bad their hangovers were. What matters is how much you drink overall.

**"Clear spirits never give you a hangover."** Darker drinks like whiskey, bourbon, and red wine contain more congeners (by-products of fermentation and aging), and some research links these to worse hangovers. But a large amount of vodka will still give you a hangover. Spirit color is a minor factor compared with quantity.

**"I'll sober up quickly with coffee."** Coffee can make you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol. You end up as a more awake drunk person, which can make you misjudge how impaired you are.

**"Eating a big meal at the end of the night soaks it up."** Late-night food can make you feel better, but once alcohol is absorbed into your bloodstream, eating doesn't remove it. Food helps most when it's in your stomach before and during drinking.

**"A painkiller before bed prevents the headache."** Taking acetaminophen while alcohol is still in your system adds to your liver's workload, and there's no good evidence it prevents a hangover. Deal with a headache in the morning, after you've eaten.

## Where Supplements Fit (and Where They Don't)

Some people look for a supplement to take before a holiday party. Here's an honest take: nothing replaces eating, pacing, and drinking less. No pill makes five cocktails behave like two, and no supplement makes it safe to drive after drinking.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven. Some people take it before or during a night out as one part of a broader plan alongside food, water, and pacing. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts, and if you take any regular medication, check with a pharmacist first.

## Your Office Holiday Party Checklist

**Before:**
- Eat a proper meal an hour or two beforehand
- Drink water through the afternoon
- Set a drink limit you'd be comfortable with your boss seeing
- Arrange your ride home
- Check whether any of your medications interact with alcohol

**During:**
- First drink is non-alcoholic
- Alternate every alcoholic drink with water or a soft drink
- One drink at a time; make each one last
- Choose simple, measurable drinks; skip punch and shots
- Keep eating
- Check in with yourself at the halfway point

**After:**
- Think twice about the after-party
- Get home safely, never by driving yourself after drinking
- Water and a snack before bed
- Breakfast, fluids, and on time to work the next day

For more seasonal strategies, see our [holiday drinking survival guide](/never-hungover/holiday-drinking-survival-guide-health-first-approach) and our general [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips). If New Year's Eve is next on your calendar, our [New Year's hangover guide](/never-hungover/new-years-hangover) has you covered.

## The Bottom Line

The office holiday party is a chance to connect with colleagues and celebrate the year, and drinking can be part of that. The open bar, the empty stomach, the nerves, and the constant refills are what trip people up. Eat first, start with a non-alcoholic drink, alternate with water, keep it to a number you've chosen in advance, skip the shots, and know how you're getting home. That's the whole plan. Do that and you'll enjoy the night, remember every conversation, and walk into work the next morning feeling fine.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How many drinks should I have at a work Christmas party?**

There's no universal number, but two or three standard drinks spread over a three- or four-hour event is a sensible range for many adults. Choose a limit before you arrive that you'd be comfortable with your manager seeing, eat beforehand, and alternate each drink with water. If you're driving, taking medication that interacts with alcohol, or pregnant, the right number is zero.

**How do I not get drunk at the office holiday party?**

Eat a real meal before you go, make your first drink non-alcoholic, and alternate every alcoholic drink with water or a soft drink. Hold one drink at a time, choose simple measurable drinks like beer, a glass of wine, or a single-shot highball, and skip shots and punch. Check in with yourself halfway through and switch to non-alcoholic drinks once you reach your limit.

**How do I pace myself at an open bar?**

Treat each drink as needing to last about an hour, since your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour. Alternate with water, don't accept a new drink until you've finished the current one, and watch for servers topping up your wine glass. Keep eating throughout the night, and stay away from rounds of shots, which add drinks quickly.

**How do I politely turn down a drink at a work party?**

Keep it short and friendly: "I'm driving," "I've got an early start," or "I'm good for now, thanks." Holding a non-alcoholic drink like sparkling water with lime is the easiest way to avoid questions entirely. You don't owe anyone an explanation, and many colleagues are pacing themselves too.

**What should I eat before an office Christmas party?**

A normal meal with protein, some fat, and fiber, eaten an hour or two before you arrive, such as a chicken and grain bowl, eggs and toast, or a sandwich and soup. Food in your stomach slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed. Keep eating the more substantial appetizers through the evening too.

**Is it OK to go to the after-party?**

It can be, but it's where many work nights go wrong: you're already a few drinks in, the event's structure is gone, and it's getting late. If you go, switch to non-alcoholic drinks or set a strict one-drink limit, and head home at a reasonable time if you have work the next day.

**What should I do if a coworker drinks too much?**

If they're unsteady but responsive, steer them toward food and water and help them get a safe ride home, never letting them drive. If they can't be woken, are breathing slowly or irregularly, have a seizure, have blue or very pale skin, or are vomiting while barely conscious, call 911 right away. Don't leave them alone, and roll them onto their side if they're lying down.

**Can I take anything before a holiday party to avoid a hangover?**

Nothing replaces eating, pacing, and drinking less. Some people take DHM, a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, as part of a broader plan, but the human evidence is limited and there is no good evidence that any supplement prevents a hangover after heavy drinking. Don't take acetaminophen before or during drinking, and check with a pharmacist if you take regular medication.
